tagline: The fish that looks up through its own forehead
summary: A small twilight-zone fish whose glowing green, tube-shaped eyes sit inside a transparent, fluid-filled shield on its head. It hovers almost motionless, scanning the faint light above for the silhouettes of prey, then rotates its eyes forward to feed.
ability: rotating tubular eyes inside a see-through head

stats.size: Up to about 15 cm
stats.range: North Pacific, from the Bering Sea to Japan and Baja California
stats.diet: Zooplankton, including small crustaceans and siphonophores

facts.title: A see-through head
facts.text: A transparent, fluid-filled shield covers the top of the head. It was missing from most older descriptions, probably because the fragile dome was destroyed when fish were hauled up in nets.

facts.title: Eyes that swivel
facts.text: Its tubular eyes were long thought to be fixed, staring only upward. Robison and Reisenbichler (2008) used ROV video and a live, net-caught fish to show the eyes rotate forward as the fish tilts to feed.

facts.title: Green sunglasses
facts.text: The tubular eyes are capped by bright green lenses. MBARI suggests the green pigment filters out direct sunlight, helping the fish pick out the bioluminescent glow of prey overhead.

facts.title: Hovering hunter
facts.text: Large, flat fins let it hang nearly motionless and manoeuvre precisely. Its pointed mouth is small, but its gut is large, and two net-caught fish had jelly fragments in their stomachs.

facts.title: Thief among tentacles?
facts.text: Researchers speculate it may pick prey out of the stinging tentacles of siphonophores (colonial jellies), with its clear shield protecting its eyes from stings — an idea still to be confirmed.

references.title: Researchers solve mystery of deep-sea fish with tubular eyes and transparent head
Robison, B.H. & Reisenbichler, K.R. (2008). Macropinna microstoma and the paradox of its tubular eyes. Copeia 2008(4): 780–784

image.alt: A small black fish lying on an open palm; the front of its head is a clear dome through which a large dark eye is visible.
image.caption: A barreleye collected by trawl in the Gulf of Alaska during a NOAA Ocean Exploration expedition; its clear head shield is still intact.
image.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Exploring Pelagic Biodiversity of the Gulf of Alaska and the Impact of Its Seamounts (author not named)

notes: Only one licence-compatible Commons image of M. microstoma exists (fresh trawl specimen held in a hand, NOAA public domain; Commons file description says 'a barreleye fish (Opisthoproctidae)' but it is filed in Category:Macropinna microstoma and the transparent head shield and tubular eyes match). MBARI's in-situ ROV images are copyrighted. 'Barreleye' is also used for other Opisthoproctidae. Conservation status per FishBase (IUCN Not Evaluated). WoRMS places the family in Argentiniformes; class given as Teleostei per WoRMS.

tagline: By day a tight fist, by night a living plankton net
summary: A relative of brittle stars whose arms fork again and again into a fine, tangled mesh. By day it hides curled into a ball. At night it climbs to a high perch on a coral or sea fan and opens into a net close to a metre across to catch plankton drifting on the current.

stats.size: Arms spread to nearly 1 m across
stats.depth: Shallow water, down to about 30 m
stats.range: Western Atlantic, from North Carolina to Brazil, including the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico
stats.diet: Plankton, small shrimps and even juvenile fishes

facts.title: Branching arms
facts.text: Like other echinoderms it is built on five rays. In basket stars these arms split again and again into ever finer branches, a trait found only in the order Euryalida.

facts.title: A net that closes
facts.text: When a tiny branch touches food, the smallest branchlets curl around it to form a ball, which is passed to the mouth. Small shrimps and juvenile fish can be caught this way.

facts.title: Microscopic grabbers
facts.text: Its arms are ringed with bands of pedicellariae, tiny grasping structures that in this family help catch prey.

facts.title: Shy of torchlight
facts.text: Shine a light on a feeding basket star at night and it slowly curls up. Within several minutes it shrinks into a fist-sized bundle.

facts.title: Feeds facing the flow
facts.text: It feeds only when conditions suit. In moderate currents it spreads its arms and turns them toward the flow, but it keeps them folded when the current is too strong.

references.title: A Sister-Group Comparison of Branching and Pedicellariae in Brittlestars (Echinodermata: Ophiuroidea) — 2023

image.alt: Top view of a basket star on a black background. A small, spotted orange central disc gives rise to arms that fork repeatedly into fine, coiling, salmon-pink branches spreading across the whole frame.
image.caption: A giant basket star photographed by the Florida Museum of Natural History, showing its repeatedly forking arms.
image.creator: François Michonneau

gallery.alt: At night on a reef, a basket star perched on a boulder coral spreads a huge orange, lace-like fan of finely branching arms, with its coiled central body at the middle.
gallery.caption: Fully spread for night-time feeding on a reef in Panama.
gallery.creator: A H (via iNaturalist)

notes: We chose Astrophyton muricatum over Gorgonocephalus: Commons has very few live Gorgonocephalus photos and many good, correctly placed Astrophyton ones. Astrophyton is monotypic, which makes its ID easier. Two Diego Delso photos labelled A. muricatum from the Red Sea (Egypt; Jeddah, Saudi Arabia) were REJECTED as misidentified, because this species is western Atlantic only. The hero is a Florida Museum (FLMNH) photograph by echinoderm researcher F. Michonneau, probably a freshly collected animal; the setting is assumed to be 'specimen'. Gallery caveat: the iNaturalist image is from Panama, which has both Atlantic and Pacific coasts. The coral looks Caribbean, but please verify the observation locality before publishing. Wikipedia states 'eight arms'; we did not use that because basket stars have five branched rays (PMC 2023). The 'giants' category rests on the ~1 m arm spread and the common name 'giant basket star'; drop it if you want a stricter reading. Most behavioural facts come from Wikipedia, citing Jangoux 1990 (Echinoderm Research).

tagline: A giant cape-wearing female and a walnut-sized male
summary: The violet blanket octopus drifts in warm open seas, never resting on the seafloor. Females unfurl a vast, colourful web of skin between their arms like a cape, and can grow to about 2 m, while males stay only a few centimetres long: one of the most extreme size gaps between the sexes in any large animal.

stats.size: Females up to about 2 m; males about 2.4 cm
stats.range: Warm seas worldwide
stats.diet: Carnivore

facts.title: Extreme size gap
facts.text: Females can reach about 2 m long while males stay around 2.4 cm. By weight the sexes differ by a factor of at least 10,000; National Geographic puts it as high as 40,000.

facts.title: A cape for defence
facts.text: When threatened, a female spreads the sheets of webbing between her arms to look far bigger. The web can also tear away if a predator bites it, letting her escape.

facts.title: Borrowed stingers
facts.text: Small blanket octopuses have been seen carrying torn-off tentacles of the Portuguese man o' war, likely brandished as weapons. How they handle the stinging cells is not fully understood.

facts.title: A detachable arm
facts.text: The tiny male stores sperm in a special arm (the hectocotylus), which he detaches and gives to the female. She keeps it in her body until she is ready to fertilise her eggs.

facts.title: Males rarely seen
facts.text: Males are so small and elusive that the first live male was not seen by scientists until 2002, off the Great Barrier Reef.

image.alt: Hand-coloured 19th-century plate of a female blanket octopus seen from above, a pale blue body with two long arms joined by a broad pinkish web spreading upward like a cape
image.caption: Female violet blanket octopus, a hand-coloured plate by Jean Baptiste Vérany (19th century)
image.creator: Jean Baptiste Vérany

notes: No freely licensed in-situ underwater photo of T. violaceus on Commons; available photos are beach-stranded/handheld specimens (South Padre Island), a museum jar, or multi-panel ZooKeys figures. Used Vérany's public-domain plate (portrait, includes plate margins/text). Tremoctopus robsoni photo rejected (different species). The NatGeo page covers the genus (Tremoctopus spp.); size ratio sources differ (10,000 vs 40,000 by weight) — both given. Wikipedia attributes the size/dimorphism and first-live-male facts to Norman et al. 2002 (NZ J. Mar. Freshw. Res.), and IUCN LC to Allcock 2014. Whether the octopus is immune to man o' war stings is disputed (NatGeo says immune; Wikipedia says unknown), so framed as hypothesis.

tagline: Not ugly—just out of its depth
summary: Famous as the 'world's ugliest animal', the smooth-head blobfish only looks like a melted frown after being hauled up from the deep. At home on the seafloor 600–1,200 m down, its soft body is held in shape by the pressure and it looks like a plump, ordinary fish.

stats.size: Up to about 38 cm
stats.range: Continental slope off southern and south-eastern Australia, including Tasmania
stats.diet: Not well documented

facts.title: The famous face is damage
facts.text: The viral 'blob' photo shows a decompressed dead specimen. Hauled up rapidly from over a kilometre down, the fish's jelly-like body collapses at the surface, distorting its features.

facts.title: Built for pressure
facts.text: Blobfish have no swim bladder and very soft, barely hardened bones. That lets them withstand crushing deep-sea pressure without cracking—but leaves nothing to hold their shape in air.

facts.title: What it really looks like
facts.text: Alive and at the right pressure it is probably far more fish-like, as the original 1926 drawing shows: plump and soft-bodied, but with normal fins and a recognisable face.

facts.title: A 'withered' name
facts.text: Marcidus is Latin for withered or weak, probably because its head, body and fins are covered in loose, flabby skin that hides the features beneath.

facts.title: Which blob was 'Mr Blobby'?
facts.text: The famous 2003 specimen, nicknamed Mr Blobby and kept at the Australian Museum, was trawled off New Zealand. It is only 'possibly' this species; some sources assign it to a close relative.

references.title: 'World's ugliest animal' contest took a blobfish out of water

image.alt: Black-and-white drawing of a soft-bodied fish with a large rounded head, big eye, wide mouth, broad fan-like pectoral fin, long dorsal and anal fins and a rounded tail.
image.caption: The original illustration from McCulloch's 1926 description of the species, drawn from a trawled specimen: far more fish-like than the famous 'blob' photo.
image.creator: Allan Riverstone McCulloch (Biological Results of the F.I.S. Endeavour)

notes: No licence-compatible photograph of P. marcidus exists on Commons; the famous 'Mr Blobby' photo (Kerryn Parkinson/NORFANZ) is copyrighted. Hero is the type illustration (McCulloch 1926, Endeavour results pl. LV fig. 2 — matches the citation in Fishes of Australia); it is only 1000×395 px and was NOT upscaled, so it needs a contained/letterboxed layout rather than a full-bleed crop. Rejected: 'Two Psychrolutes marcidus.jpg' (Rachel Caauwe, CC BY-SA 3.0) — a modern artist's imaginative painting labelled 'in situ', not a scientific record; 'Foul disease' (whiteboard graffiti); 'CBNMS Blob Sculpin' (different species, Psychrolutes phrictus). Diet: no fetched source documented it, hence 'Not well documented'. Mr Blobby's ID: Science News says 'possibly' P. marcidus; BBC Science Focus says P. microporos. Range per Fishes of Australia ('endemic'); some sources extend it to New Zealand. WoRMS order is Perciformes (older sources: Scorpaeniformes). 'Ugliest animal' title from the 2013 Ugly Animal Preservation Society vote.

tagline: An upside-down sea slug that steals stingers from its prey
summary: A small nudibranch about 3 cm long that floats belly-up at the ocean surface, buoyed by a swallowed air bubble. It eats venomous drifters such as the Portuguese man o' war and stores their unfired stinging cells in its finger-like cerata, turning its prey's weapons into its own defence.

stats.size: Usually about 3 cm long
stats.range: Open ocean, tropical to temperate waters worldwide; often washed ashore
stats.diet: Floating cnidarians such as bluebottles/men o' war, by-the-wind sailors and blue buttons; also fish in lab trials

facts.title: Floats upside down
facts.text: Air swallowed into its stomach keeps it at the surface, belly-side up. Its blue underside faces the sky, while its silvery back faces the deep.

facts.title: Camouflage both ways
facts.text: Its colouring is countershading: from above, the blue blends with the sea, and from below, the silver-grey blends with the bright surface.

facts.title: Borrowed weapons
facts.text: It eats Physalia and other floating cnidarians and stores their stinging capsules, called nematocysts, in sacs at the tips of its cerata. This theft is called kleptocnidae. Handling one can cause a painful sting.

facts.title: Cerata used as hands
facts.text: In 2025 researchers filmed captive blue dragons using their front cerata like arms to grab whitebait and jellyfish. This suggests they are more generalist hunters than once thought.

facts.title: Look-alike species
facts.text: A similar blue dragon once lumped as Glaucus marginatus turned out to be four separate species. Genetic studies show that G. atlanticus populations are separated by ocean basins.

references.title: Blue angels have devil hands: Predatory behavior using cerata in Glaucus atlanticus (2025)

image.alt: Top-down view of a blue dragon sea slug in shallow water. Its slender body has a dark blue stripe and pale blue-white sides, and three pairs of fan-like clusters of pointed blue-and-white cerata spread out from it like wings, over a blurred olive-green rock.
image.caption: A blue dragon washed ashore at Bronte Beach, Sydney, photographed in a rock pool.
image.creator: Sylke Rohrlach

notes: Setting: a stranded animal photographed in a shallow rock pool, not its true open-ocean habitat. The photographer labels the animal G. atlanticus. Note that the G. marginatus complex also occurs off Sydney and looks similar, so photo IDs carry some uncertainty. Some Commons images show G. marginatus or G. bennettae alongside G. atlanticus; we avoided those. The 'venomous' category reflects its stolen nematocysts, which can sting humans; the slug itself does not make venom. We did NOT use the popular claim that it stings 'more powerfully than the man o' war' (Wikipedia), because it is weakly supported. Size, countershading and the cryptic-species details come from Wikipedia, which cites Churchill et al. 2014.

tagline: A pocket-sized octopus with a lethal warning sign
summary: Barely the size of a golf ball, the greater blue-ringed octopus hides camouflaged among reef rubble. Disturb it and about 60 electric-blue rings flash on its skin: a warning backed by tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison potent enough to kill a human.

stats.size: Up to about 10 cm, arms included
stats.range: Tropical and subtropical Indo-West Pacific, from Sri Lanka to the Philippines, Australia and Vanuatu
stats.diet: Small crabs, shrimps and molluscs

facts.title: Rings that switch on
facts.text: Its roughly 60 blue rings contain mirror-like layered reflectors. Muscles, under direct nerve control, open and close skin around each ring to flash it in a fraction of a second: a mechanism not known in other cephalopods.

facts.title: Tetrodotoxin venom
facts.text: Its bite can deliver tetrodotoxin (TTX), the same nerve poison found in pufferfish. TTX blocks the channels nerves use to fire, causing paralysis, and there is no known antidote.

facts.title: Who makes the poison?
facts.text: Bacteria living in the octopus's salivary glands have been proposed as the true source of its TTX, but early evidence was weak and the question remains open.

facts.title: Bluff first, bite last
facts.text: It spends most of its time hidden and well camouflaged. It flashes its rings when disturbed and bites only when strongly harassed, so it is dangerous mainly to people who handle it.

facts.title: A mother's last clutch
facts.text: The female carries her clutch of eggs beneath her arms until they hatch, not feeding during that time, and dies soon after.

references.title: How does the blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena lunulata) flash its blue rings? (Mäthger et al. 2012, J. Exp. Biol.)
Distribution of Tetrodotoxin in Blue-Ringed Octopuses and the Hunt for Tetrodotoxin-Producing Symbiotic Bacteria (Williams 2009, The Malacologist)

image.alt: A small yellow octopus covered in vivid blue rings outlined in black, perched on a dark, fuzzy reef bottom
image.caption: Greater blue-ringed octopus showing its warning rings, Lembeh Strait, Indonesia
image.creator: Rickard Zerpe

gallery.alt: A pale blue-ringed octopus on a reef, its body curled forward over a clutch of eggs held beneath its arms
gallery.caption: A female greater blue-ringed octopus brooding eggs, Lembeh, Indonesia
gallery.creator: Rickard Zerpe

notes: Venom confirmed as tetrodotoxin (TTX). The Mäthger et al. abstract (PubMed) states the neurotoxin can kill a human; the 'no antidote' and brooding details come from Wikipedia (secondary). Clutch size and brooding duration vary between sources (Wikipedia gives both 50–100 and 60–100 eggs, ~1 month and ~50 days), so no numbers used. Depth: sources say 'shallow waters'; depthRange 0–20 m is an approximation for the gauge. Rings in the alt photo: whether the eggs are visible is subtle in the frame; the Commons title states 'with eggs'.

tagline: A buried ambush hunter with spring-loaded jaws
summary: A giant bristle worm that hides almost its whole body in a mucus-lined burrow, leaving only five striped antennae above the sand. When a fish touches them, its jaws snap shut and drag the prey underground. Recorded specimens approach 3 m long, which makes it a contender for the longest polychaete.

stats.size: Longest recorded specimen about 3 m (299 cm)
stats.depth: Shallow, warm coastal seabeds: intertidal to subtidal sand, rubble and rock
stats.range: Warm waters of the Indo-Pacific and Atlantic (identity of many records uncertain)
stats.diet: Fishes and other passing animals

facts.title: Antennae as bait
facts.text: By day it lies buried with five striped antennae poking out. These sense passing prey and may also work as a lure. Its jaws wait under tension like a sprung trap.

facts.title: Changes tactics at night
facts.text: After dark, it switches from waiting to actively hunting, pushing out of its burrow to snatch passing prey.

facts.title: Fish fight back
facts.text: In Indonesia's Lembeh Strait, groups of young monocle bream were seen 'mobbing' bobbit worms, squirting jets of water at the burrow until the worm sometimes retreated.

facts.title: A 20-million-year-old lair
facts.text: L-shaped fossil burrows up to 2 m long, found in Miocene rocks in Taiwan, closely resemble bobbit worm lairs. They suggest ambush-hunting worms like this were already present about 20 million years ago.

facts.title: Probably several species
facts.text: Many different giant worms have been lumped under this name. Taxonomists warn that some 'bobbit worms' worldwide may be other, even undescribed, species.

references.title: Novel mobbing strategies of a fish population against a sessile annelid predator — Lachat & Haag-Wackernagel 2016
A new species of giant Eunice (Eunicidae, Polychaeta, Annelida) from the east coast of Australia (2022)
The 20-million-year old lair of an ambush-predatory worm preserved in northeast Taiwan (2021)

image.alt: The head of a large worm rising from dark gravelly sand. Its tan, iridescent body segments shimmer blue and green, curved grey jaws spread open, and five striped antennae stick straight up.
image.caption: A bobbit worm with its jaws open, Anilao, Philippines.
image.creator: Rickard Zerpe

notes: WoRMS gives Eunice aphroditois (Pallas, 1788) as the accepted name. Its type locality is Sri Lanka and no type specimen exists. Per the ZooKeys 2022 paper, Indo-Pacific 'bobbit worms' are almost always identified as E. aphroditois, but this name has absorbed several giant species. The hero photo (Philippines) follows that convention; its true species identity cannot be confirmed from a photo. Commons iNaturalist images of slim reddish worms on rock, and a fish-like image ('Eunice aphroditois 33864655'), were rejected. The 299 cm figure is the record specimen cited in Lachat & Haag-Wackernagel 2016. We did not use the popular story that the name refers to females severing males' genitals: no source supports it. Depth is not given in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–40 m is an indicative value for shallow coastal habitat.

tagline: A living link to the age before dinosaurs
summary: The chambered nautilus is a cephalopod that still carries its ancestors' coiled, striped shell, divided into gas-filled chambers that keep it afloat. It rises at night from deep reef slopes to hunt with more than 90 sticky tentacles, and lives for 20 years or more, which makes it slow to recover from shell collecting.

stats.size: Shell typically about 13–23 cm across
stats.depth: Down to about 700 m by day; up to about 70 m at night
stats.range: Western Pacific and coastal Indian Ocean
stats.diet: Fishes and crustaceans such as crabs and shrimps; also scavenges
stats.conservation: US Endangered Species Act: Threatened; CITES Appendix II (IUCN status not found)

facts.title: An ancient design
facts.text: Nautiluses have changed little over about 150 million years and were cruising deep reefs before the dinosaurs, earning them the label 'living fossil'.

facts.title: A shell that floats
facts.text: Its body sits in the outermost chamber. A tube called the siphuncle runs through the older chambers, letting the animal adjust the gas and liquid inside them to control buoyancy.

facts.title: Ninety-plus tentacles
facts.text: It has more than 90 tentacles, the most of any cephalopod. They have no suckers; instead, grooves, ridges and a sticky coating grip prey, and chemical sensors smell food in the water.

facts.title: Daily commute
facts.text: By day it lingers on deep reef slopes to avoid predators, as deep as about 700 m; at night it rises to around 70 m to feed and lay eggs.

facts.title: Slow life, real threat
facts.text: Nautiluses mature at roughly 10–15 years and lay few eggs. Fishing for the international shell trade is their main threat; the US listed the species as threatened in 2018.

image.alt: A chambered nautilus against a black background, its cream shell striped with brown, a spotted hood above a small eye, and a cluster of pale tentacles reaching forward
image.caption: Chambered nautilus at Pairi Daiza, Brugelette, Belgium
image.creator: Hans Hillewaert

notes: Aquarium photo; the only in-situ Commons image (Dunstan et al. ROV frame) is small (1767 px) with caption panels. MBA says ESA listing in 2017, NOAA Fisheries says 2018 (final rule was 2018) — used 2018. Shell size: MBA 16–21 cm diameter vs NOAA 5–9 in (13–23 cm) at maturity; used the NOAA range. Maturity: MBA 12–15 yr, NOAA 10–15 yr. The siphuncle fact is phrased from NOAA's description (which calls the tube the 'hyponome', a term usually used for the funnel; I used 'siphuncle', the standard anatomical term) — editor may wish to verify wording. Nautilus taxonomy is unsettled (NOAA). IUCN status for N. pompilius not found in fetched sources.

tagline: Twin spiral crowns on a worm that lives inside living coral
summary: The colourful 'trees' are all most divers ever see of this worm. They are twin spiral crowns of feathery tentacles that strain food from the water and help it breathe. The rest of the worm stays hidden in a limy tube buried in living coral, and it snaps back inside and shuts a spiny trapdoor when danger approaches.
ability: spiral feeding crowns and trapdoor retreat

stats.size: Body about 3.8 cm; tube up to about 20 cm long
stats.range: Caribbean and tropical western Atlantic (similar worms in the Indo-Pacific are now often treated as separate species)
stats.diet: Plankton and other tiny particles filtered from the water

facts.title: Trees made of tentacles
facts.text: Each 'tree' is a spiral of feathery tentacles called radioles. Cilia on them carry trapped food to the mouth, and they double as gills.

facts.title: A spiny trapdoor
facts.text: When startled, the worm retreats into its tube and seals the entrance with an operculum: a hard, calcified lid armed with antler-shaped spines.

facts.title: Living inside coral
facts.text: Larvae settle on living coral and build a calcareous tube. The coral then grows around the tube until only the opening shows.

facts.title: Some live for decades
facts.text: By counting the host coral's annual growth bands, researchers estimated that some worms had lived more than 10 years and a few more than 40 years.

facts.title: Not always a good tenant
facts.text: Christmas tree worms' moving lids can rub and wound the coral around them, especially when algae grow on the lid. In a Thai survey of related Indo-Pacific species, about a fifth of the lids examined had caused visible injuries.

references.title: Filamentous turf algae on tube worms intensify damage in massive Porites corals — Hoeksema et al. 2019
Age-estimation of the Christmas Tree Worm Spirobranchus giganteus living buried in the coral skeleton from the coral-growth band of the host coral — Nishi & Nishihira 1996

image.alt: Two white-and-purple spiral crowns of a Christmas tree worm rising side by side from the top of a domed orange brain coral, against a soft green background.
image.caption: A Christmas tree worm's twin crowns emerging from a brain coral off San Pedro, Belize.
image.creator: Diego Delso

notes: TAXONOMY CAUTION: In the strict sense, S. giganteus is the Caribbean/western Atlantic Christmas tree worm. Indo-Pacific 'Christmas tree worms' are now mostly assigned to S. corniculatus and related species; the Thai survey (ref 2) found S. corniculatus, S. richardsmithi and S. cf. tetraceros. However, WoRMS distribution records and Wikipedia still list Indo-Pacific localities for S. giganteus. We therefore chose a Caribbean (Belize) photo and rejected the many Indo-Pacific Commons images filed under S. giganteus (Thailand, Philippines, Fiji, Red Sea, etc.) as doubtful IDs. A g. phua photo from Cuba was also good but carries a watermark. The age study (ref 3, Japanese authors, 1996) used the name S. giganteus before the Indo-Pacific split. It may concern an Indo-Pacific species of the complex; the abstract does not give the locality. CATEGORIES left empty: none of the allowed categories (deep-sea, bioluminescent, intelligent, camouflage, giants, venomous, transparent, reproduction, ancient) is sourced for this species; the editor may decide. Depth is not documented in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–30 m is an indicative value for shallow reef. Body and tube sizes come from Wikipedia.

tagline: The fish that came back from extinction
summary: A large, slow-living fish with fleshy, limb-like fins, from a lineage thought extinct for 70 million years until a living specimen turned up in 1938. Dark metallic blue with pale spots, it shelters in deep rocky caves by day and drifts out to feed at night. It may live nearly a century.
ability: fleshy lobed fins and an ultra-slow life

stats.size: Up to about 2 m and 95 kg
stats.range: Western Indian Ocean: the Comoros, with populations off South Africa, Madagascar and Mozambique
stats.diet: Fishes and squid

facts.title: Back from the dead
facts.text: Its lineage of lobe-finned fishes was thought to have died out 70 million years ago, until a living coelacanth was discovered in 1938. Modern coelacanths look remarkably like many fossil relatives.

facts.title: Not our closest fishy cousin
facts.text: Sequencing its genome in 2013 showed that lungfish, not the coelacanth, are the closest living relatives of four-limbed animals—though it still offers clues to how fins became limbs.

facts.title: A century-long life
facts.text: By counting tiny annual growth marks on scales, a 2021 study found the oldest specimen was 84 years old and estimated maturity at around 55. Earlier work had assumed lifespans of about 20 years.

facts.title: A five-year pregnancy
facts.text: Coelacanths give birth to live young. The same 2021 study suggests embryos develop for about five years inside the mother—earlier estimates were around three years, already among the longest of any vertebrate.

facts.title: Cave sleepers, night drifters
facts.text: By day they rest in caves on steep rocky slopes—up to 14 in one cave. At night they forage alone, drifting with currents and travelling up to about 8 km before retreating at dawn.

references.title: Amemiya, C.T. et al. (2013). The African coelacanth genome provides insights into tetrapod evolution. Nature 496: 311–316
Coelacanths may live nearly a century, five times longer than researchers expected (on Mahé, Ernande & Herbin 2021, Current Biology)
Mahé, K., Ernande, B. & Herbin, M. (2021). New scale analyses reveal centenarian African coelacanths. Current Biology

image.alt: A large, heavy-bodied fish with thick, fleshy, paddle-like fins and a three-lobed tail, displayed against a deep blue background and lit in blue.
image.caption: A preserved coelacanth on display at the Musée zoologique de Strasbourg, France. The blue is the display lighting, though in life the fish is a dark metallic blue with pale spots.
image.creator: Ji-Elle (Wikimedia Commons)

notes: No freely licensed in-situ photograph exists on Commons (live footage by Fricke/Ballesta etc. is copyrighted). Hero is a taxidermied/preserved museum specimen (Strasbourg) under blue display light. Rejected: Sebastian Brandt 3D 'zoological reconstruction' images (models), 'Smith with the second coelacanth…-transformed.png' (filename suggests digital transformation/upscaling of a historical photo). The 1938 specimen was from South Africa; IUCN Critically Endangered per FishBase (assessment dated 2000). Fact refs: fact 0 and 1 cite the Nature genome paper (index 2); facts 2–3 cite the EurekAlert release (index 3) with the paper (index 4) also listed. Gestation estimates differ: FishBase ~3 years; Mahé et al. 2021 ~5 years. Authority per WoRMS: Smith, 1939.

tagline: The heaviest invertebrate on Earth
summary: A giant of the icy Southern Ocean, the colossal squid is the heaviest known invertebrate, armed with rotating hooks on its tentacles and the largest eyes ever studied. For a century it was known almost only from whale stomachs and fishing catches, until a baby was filmed alive in 2025.

stats.size: Estimated up to about 7 m long and 500 kg
stats.depth: Adults about 1,000 m or deeper; juveniles shallower
stats.range: Antarctic waters, reaching north to southern New Zealand
stats.diet: Fishes, including Antarctic toothfish

facts.title: Heavyweight champion
facts.text: A colossal squid caught in the Ross Sea in 2007 weighed about 470–495 kg, and scientists estimate the species reaches about 500 kg, making it the heaviest invertebrate known.

facts.title: Hooks that turn
facts.text: The club-shaped tips of its two tentacles carry rotating hooks, and its arms bear hooks too. No other glass squid has them.

facts.title: Record-breaking eyes
facts.text: It has the largest animal eyes ever studied, possibly the largest of any animal in history, useful for spotting faint light in the deep.

facts.title: First seen alive in 2025
facts.text: In March 2025 a remotely operated vehicle filmed a see-through, 30 cm juvenile at 600 m near the South Sandwich Islands: the first confirmed footage of a live colossal squid in its habitat.

facts.title: Whale food
facts.text: Beaks pile up in sperm whale stomachs because they resist digestion. From these, scientists estimate colossal squid could make up a large share of some sperm whales' diet in the Southern Ocean.

references.title: Colossal squid (Colossal squid at Te Papa; Anatomy; Life and habits)
references.publisher: Te Papa — Museum of New Zealand

references.title: First Confirmed Footage of a Colossal Squid—and it's a Baby!

image.alt: A preserved colossal squid lying in a long glass display tank, its broad fin at the top and thick orange-pink arms hanging down through the fluid
image.caption: The colossal squid on display at Te Papa, Wellington: the only one on public display in the world, caught in the Ross Sea in 2007
image.creator: Scotted400

notes: Image is a portrait museum display photo (Te Papa specimen); crop for landscape will be tight. Rejected: Commons 'Colossal squid head and limbs, NHM' tank photos (could not verify these are not the NHM's giant squid), 'Giant Squid (20495944085)' (comparison with giant squid tentacle), and size-comparison illustrations. Te Papa's 'life and habits' page still says nobody has seen a live colossal squid swimming; that is outdated since the 2025 Schmidt Ocean footage. Depth range is approximate (Te Papa: 1,000 m or more; Wikipedia: juveniles 0–500 m, adolescents 500–2,000 m). IUCN LC from Wikipedia infobox.

tagline: Rainbow-rippling, glass-clear and no relation to jellyfish
summary: Comb jellies are not jellyfish: they belong to their own ancient phylum, Ctenophora, and do not sting. The sea walnut swims by beating eight rows of tiny ciliary combs. These scatter light into shimmering rainbows, which is diffraction, not glowing. When disturbed it can also produce its own light.

stats.size: Up to roughly 7–12 cm long
stats.range: Native to the western Atlantic; invasive in the Black, Caspian, Baltic and North seas
stats.diet: Zooplankton, including crustaceans, other comb jellies, fish eggs and larvae

facts.title: Rainbows, not glowing
facts.text: The flickering rainbow colours come from light diffracting off the beating comb plates (fused cilia). It happens only in ambient light and is often mistaken for bioluminescence.

facts.title: It does make light too
facts.text: Mnemiopsis is genuinely bioluminescent. It uses a photoprotein, a single complex of light-making molecules, and its comb rows give off blue-green light when disturbed.

facts.title: An invader that crashed fisheries
facts.text: Carried in ships' ballast water, it reached the Black Sea in the early 1980s. There it ate fish eggs and larvae and competed with anchovy for food, contributing to a dramatic fall in catches.

facts.title: It can grow young again
facts.text: In 2024 researchers showed that stressed adults can revert to the earlier, two-tentacled cydippid larval form and later mature and spawn again. It is the first ctenophore known to do this.

facts.title: A now-you-see-it anus
facts.text: It has no permanent anus. When waste builds up, the gut fuses with the skin to open a temporary pore, which closes again after defecation. In adults this happens about once an hour.

references.title: Reverse development in the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi — Soto-Angel & Burkhardt 2024
Bioluminescence myths: All comb jellies luminesce and they make the colors of the rainbow
references.publisher: The Bioluminescence Web Page (S. Haddock, UC Santa Barbara / MBARI)

references.title: Marine eukaryote bioluminescence: a review of species and their functional biology (2025)

image.alt: A glass-clear comb jelly against a black background, seen side-on with two large rounded oral lobes. Rows of tiny comb plates along its edges scatter light into streaks of rainbow colour.
image.caption: Sea walnut (Mnemiopsis leidyi). The rainbow streaks along its comb rows are diffracted light, not bioluminescence.
image.creator: Bruno C. Vellutini

notes: We chose Mnemiopsis leidyi because Commons has many correctly identified photos and it is documented as bioluminescent: the 2025 review lists it among photoprotein species. The hero was taken by ctenophore researcher Bruno Vellutini, filed under Category:Mnemiopsis leidyi. It is most likely a lab or aquarium shot against black (setting assumed). The animal fills most of the frame, so tight landscape crops may clip the lobes. The image is 1920×1493, uncropped. Wikipedia gives the first Black Sea record as 1982. Depth is not documented in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–30 m is an indicative value for coastal plankton. Size and the invasion history come from Wikipedia (last-resort source). The 2024 reverse-development finding is from the PNAS paper.

tagline: A cigar-sized shark that bites cookies out of whales
summary: A glowing, cigar-shaped shark only about half a metre long that attacks animals far larger than itself. It latches on with sucker-like lips, spins, and carves out a neat round plug of flesh—leaving crater wounds on tunas, dolphins, whales and seals.
ability: suction-and-spin bite that cuts round plugs of flesh

stats.size: Females up to about 56 cm; males about 42 cm
stats.depth: Recorded from the surface to about 3,500–3,700 m; below about 1,000 m by day, rising at night
stats.range: Tropical to warm-temperate oceans worldwide
stats.diet: Plugs of flesh from large fishes, sharks and marine mammals; also whole squid and crustaceans

facts.title: The cookie-cutter bite
facts.text: It sucks onto its victim with fleshy lips and throat muscles, grips with slender upper teeth, then bites with its large lower teeth and spins, cutting out a deep, circular plug.

facts.title: A glowing belly
facts.text: Except for a dark collar around the throat, its underside is covered in tiny light organs that give an even greenish glow, hiding its silhouette from below (counter-illumination).

facts.title: A collar that lures?
facts.text: Biologist Edith Widder suggested that the unlit collar looks like a small fish against the glow, luring fast predators such as tunas and dolphins close enough to be bitten.

facts.title: Teeth replaced as a set
facts.text: Its lower teeth are joined at their bases and shed as a whole row rather than one by one. It swallows the old row—possibly a way to recycle calcium.

facts.title: Daily elevator ride
facts.text: It spends the day in deep water, below about 1,000 m, and migrates toward the surface at night to feed. There are even reports of its bite marks on submarine sonar domes.

image.alt: A small, slender brown shark photographed side-on against a white background, with a dark band around the gill area, two small dorsal fins set far back and a large tail.
image.caption: A cookiecutter shark from Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean; note the dark collar behind the head.
image.creator: Hugues Evano (IFREMER, Délégation océan Indien)

gallery.alt: A hand holding a small brown shark upright by its body, its round mouth wide open to show a ring of triangular lower teeth.
gallery.caption: Head-on view showing the round mouth and the row of large triangular lower teeth used to carve out plugs of flesh.
gallery.creator: NOAA Photo Library

notes: Hero: IFREMER fresh specimen from Réunion (Commons Category:Isistius brasiliensis). Gallery: NOAA Photo Library specimen held in hand (portrait). Rejected: Smithsonian jar specimen (cluttered). The 'collar lure' fact cites Fishes of Australia's summary of Widder (1998). Fishes of Australia also reports a cookiecutter bite on a long-distance swimmer in Hawaii (Honebrink et al. 2011)—not used in facts. Depth: FishBase 0–3,700 m, Fishes of Australia 0–3,500 m.

tagline: The deepest-living octopus, flapping on ear-like fins
summary: Dumbo octopuses are a genus of soft, jelly-like deep-sea octopuses named for the two ear-like fins above their eyes. They hover and 'hop' over the abyssal seafloor, and one was filmed nearly 7 km down, deeper than any other octopus or squid ever seen.

stats.size: Hadal individuals filmed at about 35–43 cm total length
stats.range: Probably worldwide in deep, cold water
stats.diet: Small seafloor animals: worms, copepods, amphipods, isopods
stats.conservation: Not evaluated by IUCN as a genus; most species are poorly known

facts.title: Deepest octopus on record
facts.text: In 2019 a baited camera lander in the Java Trench, Indian Ocean, filmed a Grimpoteuthis at 6,957 m: the first unequivocal sighting of any cephalopod in the hadal zone (below 6,000 m).

facts.title: Fins, not jets
facts.text: Unlike most octopuses, which jet water through a siphon, dumbos swim mainly by flapping their two fins, which helps them save energy in the food-poor deep sea.

facts.title: Hop, spread, repeat
facts.text: Filmed individuals foraged in short 'hops' across the mud, landing with arms and web spread before lifting off again. One picked up a tiny isopod, then dropped it.

facts.title: Eggs left on their own
facts.text: Dumbo octopuses attach large, tough-cased eggs to deep-sea corals and do not guard them. Hatchlings emerge as fully formed juveniles able to fend for themselves.

facts.title: A tangled family tree
facts.text: Telling species apart is hard: specimens are rare and often damaged, and many key features are internal, so photos alone rarely pin down a species.

references.title: First in situ observation of Cephalopoda at hadal depths (Octopoda: Opisthoteuthidae: Grimpoteuthis sp.) — Jamieson & Vecchione 2020

image.caption: A dumbo octopus (Grimpoteuthis) swims above the deep seafloor, filmed by NOAA's remotely operated vehicle; the scientists noted damage to an arm and fin
image.creator: NOAA Okeanos Explorer Program

gallery.alt: A dumbo octopus against black water, viewed from below, with its arms coiled up beneath its pale mantle and fins out to the sides

Both photos are NOAA Okeanos Explorer frames identified by NOAA only to genus (Grimpoteuthis); no Opisthoteuthis/other cirrate images used. Fin swimming, egg and diet facts are from Wikipedia (secondary; cites Collins & Villanueva 2006). Feeding has not been directly observed in Grimpoteuthis beyond the hadal isopod pick-up.

tagline: The biggest teeth for its size of any fish
summary: A small, ultra-black fish with a gaping mouth full of fangs—proportionally the largest teeth of any fish. Growing to only about 18 cm, it drifts through the twilight and midnight zones waiting for prey to come close, sensing movement rather than seeing it.
ability: oversized fangs that fold into sockets in its head

stats.size: Up to about 18 cm
stats.depth: Mostly 500–2,000 m; young near the surface, adults recorded to about 5,000 m
stats.range: Tropical and temperate seas worldwide
stats.diet: Crustaceans when young; mainly fishes as adults

facts.title: Teeth with their own garage
facts.text: Relative to its size, the fangtooth has the largest teeth of any fish. When it shuts its mouth, the huge lower fangs slide up into sockets on either side of its brain.

facts.title: Feeling, not seeing
facts.text: Its eyes are small and its eyesight is thought to be poor. Instead it relies on the dark lateral line along its side, a row of sensors that detects tiny movements in the water.

facts.title: Ultra-black skin
facts.text: Its skin is packed with pigment that absorbs about 99.5% of the light hitting it, helping it hide in plain sight.

facts.title: A baby in disguise
facts.text: Juveniles look like a different fish: pale, big-eyed, with long horn-like spines on the head and small teeth. The name cornuta, 'horned', refers to those juvenile spines.

facts.title: Rarely seen alive
facts.text: Despite living worldwide, it is elusive: MBARI's remotely operated vehicles have spotted a fangtooth on average less than once every two years since the institute opened.

image.alt: A dead, dark-brown deep-sea fish lying on crushed ice, seen from the side, with a large head, small eye and long fang-like teeth protruding from its open mouth.
image.caption: A common fangtooth on ice, photographed in Iceland.
image.creator: Brian Suda

notes: Hero is a dead specimen on ice (Commons Category:Anoplogaster cornuta; North Atlantic, where only A. cornuta occurs). Rejected: NOAA Photo Library 'Fis01058' (sharper, fresh, but only categorised to genus Anoplogaster and from a Pacific Cobb trawl, so A. cornuta vs A. brachycera cannot be confirmed; also shows a hand and wristwatch). Size: MBARI/FishBase give max 18 cm; Monterey Bay Aquarium says up to 15.2 cm and WHOI says adults average 16 cm. The fang-socket detail: Fishes of Australia says sockets 'on either side of its brain'; WHOI describes them as on the roof of the mouth—same function, different wording. WHOI also lists 'bioluminescence: yes, on the sides', which is not supported by other sources and was not used. Order follows WoRMS (Trachichthyiformes); older sources place it in Beryciformes.

tagline: A walking light show on the seafloor
summary: A small cuttlefish of tropical sand and mud flats that walks rather than swims, ambling on its arms and fin flaps. When disturbed, it stays put and ripples with waves of dark brown, white, yellow and red: a bold display long said to warn of toxic flesh, though the evidence is mixed.

stats.size: Mantle up to about 6–8 cm
stats.range: Northern Australia and southern New Guinea to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines
stats.diet: Crustaceans and small fishes
stats.conservation: IUCN: Data Deficient (assessed as Metasepia pfefferi, 2012)

facts.title: A cuttlefish that walks
facts.text: Its cuttlebone (the buoyant internal shell) is small and lets it float only briefly, so it mostly ambles over the bottom on two arms and flaps of its fin.

facts.title: Standing its ground
facts.text: Unlike most cuttlefish, it does not dart away when threatened. It stays still, pulses its fins and flashes vivid colour waves, with red arm tips, that may warn predators off.

facts.title: Toxic? Not proven
facts.text: It is often called the only poisonous cuttlefish, based on an unpublished toxicology result. Later tests found only trace tetrodotoxin, too little to harm vertebrates, so its toxicity remains unconfirmed.

facts.title: A daytime hunter
facts.text: While most cephalopods hunt at night, it is active by day, using shifting camouflage to stalk crustaceans and small fishes.

facts.title: Eggs left to hatch
facts.text: Females cement single eggs into crevices and leave them. The eggs turn see-through as they develop, and hatchlings can already make adult colour patterns.

references.title: Cuttlefishes (Cephalopoda, Sepiidae): the bare bones—an hypothesis of relationships (Lupše et al. 2023)

image.alt: A flamboyant cuttlefish walking over pale sand and seagrass, its body mottled brown and purple with yellow-edged fins and arms tipped in bright pink-red
image.caption: Flamboyant cuttlefish crawling along the sandy bottom, Apo Reef Natural Park, Philippines
image.creator: Dmitry Domrin

notes: Name: WoRMS accepts Ascarosepion pfefferi (Hoyle, 1885); Metasepia pfefferi is a superseded combination (AphiaID 342366 → 1667026), following Lupše et al. 2023. Reference index 1 (Lupše) supports the name change only; facts 0, 1 and 3 cite the Monterey Bay Aquarium (index 2) and facts 2 and 4 cite Wikipedia (index 3). MBA still states the flesh is 'highly poisonous ... as lethal as blue-ringed octopuses' (Mark Norman, unpublished); Wikipedia reports later work finding only trace TTX. Treated as uncertain; 'venomous' category NOT assigned. Size: sources differ (6 vs 8 cm mantle). Commons file title begins with a Cyrillic 'С' (sourceUrl percent-encoded accordingly). IUCN assessment (2012) used the old name Metasepia pfefferi.

tagline: A glowing lure-tipped hat that rests by day and hunts by night
summary: A hydromedusa, not a true jellyfish, from shallow coastal waters off Japan and Korea. Its tentacles curl up over the outside of its striped bell and end in fluorescent green bands and pink tips. Experiments suggest these glowing tips may lure the small fish it eats.

stats.size: Bell up to about 15 cm across
stats.depth: Shallow coastal waters, less than about 30 m
stats.range: Northwestern Pacific: central and southern Japan, Jeju Island (South Korea)
stats.diet: Mainly small fish

facts.title: Tentacles worn on top
facts.text: Unusually, its tentacles grow up along the outside of the bell. Each one ends in a green fluorescent band and a pink-pigmented tip.

facts.title: Fluorescent fishing lures
facts.text: In lab trials, juvenile rockfish were strongly attracted to the tentacles under blue light, which makes the tips fluoresce, but not under yellow or white light. This suggests the glow works as prey bait.

facts.title: Fluorescent, not bioluminescent
facts.text: The glow is fluorescence: proteins absorb blue light and re-emit it as green. The jelly makes no light of its own.

facts.title: Day rester, night hunter
facts.text: Adults spend the day resting on the bottom among rocks or algae and rise at night to hunt. They are seen mainly from December to July, and each adult lives only a few months.

facts.title: Tentacles placed by maths
facts.text: New tentacles are added at a near-constant angle of about 137.5°, the same rule seen in plant leaf spirals. Mathematicians liken this to 'Fibonacci hashing', which spreads tentacles evenly as their number grows.

references.title: Fluorescent proteins function as a prey attractant: experimental evidence from the hydromedusa Olindias formosus and other marine organisms — Haddock & Dunn 2015
Optimal hash arrangement of tentacles in jellyfish — Okabe & Yoshimura 2016

image.alt: A dome-shaped translucent jelly on a black background. Its bell is pinstriped with dark lines and shows a peach interior, and it is ringed by many cream-coloured, pink-tipped tentacles that curl upward over the bell and trail below.
image.caption: Flower hat jelly in an aquarium. The pink-tipped tentacles curl up over its striped bell.
image.creator: Σ64

notes: The name was formerly spelled O. formosa; it was changed to formosus to correct a gender mismatch with the genus. Many popular sites also list Brazil and Argentina in its range, but sources consulted here give only Japan and Korea. South American records likely refer to a congener (e.g. O. sambaquiensis), so we left them out. Wikipedia mentions a single reported human fatality in Japan. We did not include it as a fact because it rests on a single case. Adult seasonality and day/night behaviour come from Wikipedia, which cites Patry et al. 2014 (JMBA). The setting is an aquarium; no correctly identified in situ photo was found at good resolution.

tagline: A 'flying' fish that never leaves the seabed
summary: Despite its name — volitans means 'flying' — this bottom-dwelling Atlantic fish cannot fly or even glide. It walks over sand on its pelvic fins, probing for crabs and clams, and when disturbed it suddenly fans out enormous, blue-edged pectoral fins like a pair of wings.

stats.size: Commonly about 38 cm; up to about 50 cm
stats.range: Both sides of the Atlantic, incl. the Mediterranean; Canada to Argentina in the west
stats.diet: Bottom-living crustaceans (especially crabs), clams and small fishes

facts.title: It can't fly
facts.text: Despite both its common and scientific names, the flying gurnard cannot fly or glide through the air — which is why some prefer the name 'helmet gurnard'.

facts.title: Wings as a warning?
facts.text: When excited, it spreads its huge, semi-transparent pectoral fins, edged in bright blue. Scientists suggest the sudden flash may startle predators.

facts.title: Walking the seabed
facts.text: Flying gurnards have been seen 'walking' along sandy seafloors on their pelvic fins while they search for food.

facts.title: A drumming fish
facts.text: Flying gurnards make sounds with a special drumming muscle that beats against their two-lobed swim bladder.

facts.title: Digging for dinner
facts.text: It feeds mainly on bottom-living crustaceans — especially crabs — plus clams and small fishes, using a stiff front fin ray to dig into the sediment.

image.alt: A flying gurnard seen from above on pale sand, its two huge fan-shaped pectoral fins spread wide, translucent with white spots and bright blue edges
image.caption: Fins fully fanned: a flying gurnard over sand off Menorca, Mediterranean Sea
image.creator: Encarna Sáez Goñalons & Víctor Martínez Moll

gallery.alt: Side view of a red-brown flying gurnard on sand, covered in turquoise spots, with large golden eyes, wing-like pectoral fins folded back and two tall separate spines rising from its head
gallery.caption: Wings folded: a flying gurnard propped on its fins on the seabed
gallery.creator: Barry Peters

notes: Hero location: Commons description says only 'Xoriguer' (Cala en Xoriguer, Menorca) — caption assumes Menorca. IUCN Least Concern (assessed 2013) per FishBase. Digging fact comes from Wikipedia, citing Davenport & Wirtz 2019. No allowed category clearly fits, so categories is empty.

tagline: A round, spiny angler with a glowing, tasselled lure
summary: A deep-sea anglerfish shaped like a lumpy ball. Females, up to about 60 cm long, dangle a fleshy lure lit by glowing bacteria to draw prey within reach. Males are tiny, under 5 cm, and—unlike many anglerfish—they latch on only temporarily rather than fusing for life.

stats.size: Females up to about 60 cm (standard length); males about 4 cm
stats.depth: Usually 200–800 m; recorded to about 1,830 m
stats.range: Mainly the Atlantic, from Greenland and Norway to South Africa; scattered records elsewhere
stats.diet: Fishes, squids and crustaceans

facts.title: A living lantern
facts.text: The lure (esca) on the female's head 'fishing rod' glows because it hosts light-producing bacteria. In the darkness, the light draws prey within striking distance of her mouth.

facts.title: Teeth like a trap
facts.text: Its teeth point inward, so whatever swims into the mouth struggles to get back out. Recorded prey includes fishes, squids and crustaceans.

facts.title: Tiny, independent males
facts.text: Males reach only about 4 cm, against roughly 60 cm for females. In this family males apparently do not become permanently fused 'parasites' on females, as happens in some other anglerfishes.

facts.title: A temporary grip
facts.text: Males sniff out females with large nostril organs and clamp on with special bony teeth. One female carried a scar probably left by a male that later let go.

facts.title: Prey for whales
facts.text: Despite its spines, it is eaten by sperm whales: several footballfish have been found in the stomachs of whales caught off the Azores.

references.title: A Rare Deep Sea Gem Arrives at NHM (Pacific footballfish)
references.publisher: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County

image.alt: A pale, preserved anglerfish with a rounded, lumpy body, gaping mouth and a long stalk on its head ending in a branched, tassel-like lure, against a dark background.
image.caption: A preserved female Atlantic footballfish on display at the Port of Nagoya Public Aquarium, Japan.
image.creator: KKPCW (Wikimedia Commons)

notes: Catalogue slot 'Anglerfish'. Image is the only licence-compatible Commons photo of this species: a preserved museum specimen labelled 'チョウチンアンコウ' (the Japanese standard name for H. groenlandicus) at the Port of Nagoya Public Aquarium, filed in Category:Himantolophus groenlandicus; ID rests on the aquarium label. Lure-bacteria and inward-teeth facts are from NHM LA describing the family (Pacific footballfish, H. sagamius) and apply to footballfishes generally; male non-parasitism is stated for this species by FishBase ('apparently') and for the family by NHM. Wikipedia used for range, diet, temporary-attachment and Azores sperm-whale records (it cites Pietsch 2009, Oceanic Anglerfishes). Note: the familiar 'ball-shaped anglerfish with lantern' image in Japan (chōchin-ankō) refers to this species.

tagline: An eel-shaped shark with a collar of frills
summary: A slender, eel-like shark with six frilly gill slits—the first pair meeting across the throat like a ruff—and a mouth lined with rows of small, three-pointed teeth. A primitive-looking deep-water hunter, it swallows squid, fishes and even other sharks, and may carry its young for more than a year.
ability: needle-trap jaws and an extremely long pregnancy

stats.size: Females up to almost 2 m
stats.depth: Typically 500–1,000 m; recorded from about 20 to 1,500 m
stats.range: Patchy in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, on outer shelves, slopes and seamounts
stats.diet: Deep-water squid, bony fishes and other sharks

facts.title: Where the name comes from
facts.text: It has six gill slits with frilly edges, and the lower ends of the first pair join across the throat, forming a ruff-like collar.

facts.title: Teeth that point inward
facts.text: Its large mouth holds groups of small, sharp, three-pointed teeth that point inward. It can swallow relatively large prey, including other deep-water sharks.

facts.title: A very long pregnancy
facts.text: Young hatch from eggs inside the mother and feed on large yolky eggs; litters of 2–15 pups are born at about 40–60 cm long. Gestation is thought to last more than a year.

facts.title: First filmed in 2004
facts.text: In August 2004, scientists reviewing submersible video off the south-eastern USA spotted a frilled shark gliding over sandy seafloor—thought to be the first time one was seen alive in its natural habitat.

facts.title: A 'living fossil'?
facts.text: Often called a 'living fossil', it shares many physical features with shark ancestors from the age of dinosaurs, and is described as a primitive deep-water shark.

references.title: Estuary to the Abyss 2004: August 27 log

image.caption: The frilled gill folds that give the species its name, seen on a specimen in a display tank.
image.creator: OpenCage (opencage.info)

gallery.alt: Grainy blue underwater video frame of a long, slender shark swimming over rippled sand, its shadow below, with date, depth and temperature text across the top.
gallery.caption: The first known footage of a live frilled shark in its habitat, filmed from the Johnson-Sea-Link II submersible at about 870 m (2,866 ft), 26 August 2004.
gallery.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration

notes: Hero: OpenCage close-up (Commons Category:Chlamydoselachus anguineus); the animal appears to be a dead or preserved specimen in a tank—exact location not stated on Commons. Gallery: NOAA 2004 in-situ video frame (low quality, burnt-in data overlay; depth 2,866 ft as shown on the frame). 'Living fossil' is a popular label; the NatGeo source is a photo caption.

tagline: An angler with a worm on a stick and a lightning gulp
summary: A lumpy, slow-moving anglerfish that sits motionless on the seabed, blending in, while it twitches a lure made from its first dorsal fin spine. When curious prey comes close, the frogfish's mouth snaps open and sucks it in within milliseconds — even prey nearly twice its own size.

stats.size: Commonly about 10 cm; up to about 25 cm
stats.depth: From under 1 m to over 200 m; often around 40 m
stats.range: Tropical and warm-temperate Atlantic and Indo-Pacific waters
stats.diet: Fishes and other small animals drawn in by its lure

facts.title: A fin turned fishing rod
facts.text: Its front-most dorsal fin spine has become a rod, the illicium, tipped with a bait called the esca. In this species the esca bears 2–7 worm-like appendages that wriggle like tempting prey.

facts.title: Gone in six milliseconds
facts.text: Its jaws open so suddenly that prey is sucked in along with water in about six milliseconds. High-speed filming has shown frogfishes have one of the fastest feeding mechanisms of any vertebrate.

facts.title: Eyes bigger than its stomach
facts.text: A huge mouth and stretchy stomach let it swallow prey up to twice its own size.

facts.title: Slow-motion chameleon
facts.text: Its colour is extremely variable, and over a few weeks a striated frogfish can completely change colour to match its surroundings.

facts.title: Eggs on a raft
facts.text: Its eggs are released wrapped in a ribbon-like, floating mass of mucus known as an 'egg raft'.

references.title: High-speed cinematographic evidence for ultrafast feeding in antennariid anglerfishes (Grobecker & Pietsch 1979, Science)

tagline: A pill bug the size of a dinner plate, scavenging the deep slope
summary: A distant, ocean-dwelling cousin of the garden woodlouse, scaled up enormously. Giant isopods patrol the muddy continental slopes of the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, scavenging whatever dead animals sink from above. Adults commonly measure 19–36 cm, and the largest documented is about 50 cm.

stats.size: Typically 19–36 cm; largest documented about 50 cm
stats.range: Western Atlantic: Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, and north to Georgia (USA)
stats.diet: Scavenger of dead animals sinking to the seafloor

facts.title: The largest isopod
facts.text: It is the largest known isopod. The biggest individual documented in scientific literature was about 50 cm; a widely shared 76 cm claim from the press has never been confirmed.

facts.title: Males run larger
facts.text: An analysis of historical records found that adult males are on average about 5 cm longer than females.

facts.title: Big because it's deep?
facts.text: Its large size is often explained by 'deep-sea gigantism', the tendency of some cold-water invertebrates to grow larger and live longer. The exact causes are still debated.

facts.title: Mini-adults, no larva
facts.text: Females brood eggs in a pouch called a marsupium. The young hatch as miniature adults (mancae), up to about 6 cm long, skipping a larval stage entirely.

facts.title: Eyes that shine
facts.text: Its widely spaced compound eyes have more than 4,000 facets and a reflective layer, the tapetum lucidum, that makes them seem to glow in a camera light.

references.title: Sizing ocean giants: patterns of intraspecific size variation in marine megafauna — McClain et al. 2015

image.alt: A large pale lilac isopod with a domed, segmented shell and many hooked legs walks across greenish seafloor sediment. A spiral orange whip coral curls through the foreground.
image.caption: A giant isopod beside a spiral whip coral, filmed by ROV in the Gulf of Mexico during NOAA's 2017 Okeanos Explorer expedition.
image.creator: NOAA Office of Ocean Exploration and Research

gallery.alt: Close-up underside of a freshly collected giant isopod beside a yellow measuring tape, showing long antennae, a pink head with mouthparts, hooked front legs and a cream-and-orange belly.
gallery.caption: The underside of a giant isopod collected during NOAA's 2006 Expedition to the Deep Slope (Gulf of Mexico).
gallery.creator: Expedition to the Deep Slope 2006, NOAA-OE

notes: We chose NOAA Gulf of Mexico images because records of 'B. giganteus' from the Indo-Pacific are now treated as other species (McClain 2015, citing Lowry & Dempsey 2006). Many Japanese and Taiwanese aquarium photos on Commons labelled B. giganteus may therefore show other Bathynomus species and were not used. Depth: McClain 2015 gives 310–1,800 m (one record at 80 m); Wikipedia gives 310–2,140 m for the genus in the West Atlantic. Facts 3–5 come from Wikipedia (last resort), which cites Briones-Fourzán & Lozano-Alvarez 1991 (J. Crust. Biol.). The popular story of an aquarium isopod that 'starved for five years' was deliberately not used. NOAA's swimming-isopod note (ref 1) says the animal filmed was nearly 30 cm.

tagline: The real kraken, finally caught on camera
summary: The giant squid is one of the largest invertebrates on Earth, with tentacles longer than any other cephalopod's and eyes the size of dinner plates. Known for centuries only from carcasses and sea-monster tales, it was first photographed alive in the deep sea in 2004.

stats.size: Females up to about 12–13 m total length, males about 10 m (tentacles included)
stats.range: Worldwide in temperate oceans; rare in the tropics and polar seas
stats.diet: Deep-sea fishes and squids

facts.title: First photos in the wild
facts.text: In 2004 a Japanese team's deep-sea camera photographed a giant squid attacking bait at 900 m off the Ogasawara Islands. A tentacle it left behind confirmed its identity and showed the animal was over 8 m long.

facts.title: Not 20 metres long
facts.text: Tales of 20 m giants are not backed by any measured specimen. Mantles are not known to exceed about 2.25 m; much of the length is two stretchy feeding tentacles.

facts.title: Eyes like dinner plates
facts.text: Its eyes reach at least 27 cm across, among the largest of any animal. One proposed reason is spotting the faint glow stirred up by approaching sperm whales, its main predator.

facts.title: Seen alive, and active
facts.text: Rather than a sluggish drifter, the 2004 images suggest an active predator that strikes and tangles prey with its long feeding tentacles.

facts.title: One species worldwide
facts.text: Several species were once proposed, but DNA from giant squid around the globe shows remarkably little variation, suggesting there is just one species.

references.title: First-ever observations of a live giant squid in the wild (Kubodera & Mori 2005, Proc. R. Soc. B)
Architeuthis dux (giant squid)
references.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan

image.caption: A giant squid netted by the NOAA research vessel Gordon Gunter in the Gulf of Mexico off Louisiana, now Smithsonian specimen MOL 1130046
image.creator: NOAA (credited on Commons via Paul Greenhall, Smithsonian Institution)

gallery.caption: Preserved giant squid from Skagen, Denmark (1965), Natural History Museum of Denmark, NHMD-141565
